cards.q: Describe a professional relationship.
cards.a: They are interpersonal relationships that reflect the standards of conduct expected of members in the military.

cards.q: Describe unprofessional relationships.
cards.a: Unprofessional relationships can exist between officers, between enlisted members, between officers and enlisted members, between military personnel and civilian employees, or between military members and contractor personnel.

cards.q: Summarize the policy on professional and unprofessional relationships.
cards.a: Airmen and Guardians are expected to avoid those relationships which negatively affect morale, good order and discipline, respect for authority, and unit cohesion.

cards.q: Summarize the general prohibitions relating to unprofessional relationships for officers.
cards.a: Officers must not engage in any activity with an enlisted member which reasonably may prejudice good order and discipline, discredit the armed forces or compromise the officer’s standing. It includes fraternization, failure to obey lawful orders, dereliction of duty, and conduct unbecoming an officer.

cards.q: What is fraternization (general prohibition)?
cards.a: Fraternization is a unique type of unprofessional relationship between an officer and enlisted member that is specifically criminalized in the Uniform Code of Military Justice under Article 134, Fraternization (Manual for Courts-Martial (2019), Part IV, Paragraph 83) (10 United States Code Section 934). Fraternization exists when a relationship between an officer and an enlisted member puts the enlisted member on terms of military equality with the officer in such a way that prejudices good order and discipline in the armed forces or is of a nature to bring discredit upon the armed forces. This custom of the service recognizes that officers will not form personal relationships with enlisted members on terms of military equality, whether on or off duty.

cards.q: Summarize specific prohibitions relating to unprofessional relationships for officers.
cards.a: Officers will not gamble with enlisted members, lend money to, borrow money from or otherwise become indebted to enlisted members, will not date or engage in sexual relations with enlisted members, will not engage, on a personal basis, in business enterprises with enlisted members, or solicit or make solicited sales to enlisted members.

cards.q: Summarize the effects of unprofessional relationships on unit cohesiveness.
cards.a: Erodes trust in command. Undermines obedience under stress. Weakens the authority of other leaders. Creates real or perceived favoritism, which damages morale even if no actual unfairness occurred. Confuses the chain of command's authority, since undue familiarity blurs the line between social equality and military rank/authority.

cards.q: Explain how the virtues relate to the USAF and USSF Core Values.
cards.a: Virtues are the desired behaviors and characteristics that we must practice and demonstrate. They are the behaviors that demonstrate that a person truly values the Core Values. Consistently practicing the virtues associated with the Core Values develops habits of honorable thought and action, which form the foundation of professionalism and character. Core Value = WHAT you value. Virtue/Commitment = HOW you demonstrate it.

cards.q: Describe Integrity First and its related virtues.
cards.a:
Single most important part of character
Doing the right thing, all the time
Moral compass that keeps us on the right path
Foundation upon which trust is built
Thoughts and actions align with what is right.
Its related virtues are honesty, courage, accountability, and humility.

cards.q: Describe honesty.
cards.a: This is the only way to preserve the trust we hold so dear with each other and with the population we serve

cards.q: Describe courage.
cards.a: Willingness to take personal and professional risks, make decisions that may be unpopular, and to admit to our mistakes.

cards.q: Describe accountability.
cards.a: Maintain transparency, seek honest and constructive feedback, and take ownership of actions and decisions.

cards.q: Describe humility.
cards.a: Service with gratitude and absent arrogance; putting others before ourselves as we seek to add value to our communities.

cards.q: Describe Service Before Self and its related virtues.
cards.a:
Professional duties take precedence over personal desires
Call to live to a higher standard
Commitment that takes energy, dedication, and sacrifice
Servant mindset
Embrace expectations and requirements of the profession of arms
Its related virtues are duty, loyalty, and respect.

cards.q: Describe duty.
cards.a: Consistently choosing to make necessary sacrifices to accomplish the mission and, in doing so, honoring those who make the ultimate sacrifice.

cards.q: Describe loyalty.
cards.a: Commitment to the success and preservation of something bigger than ourselves - demonstrated by helping each other act with honor.

cards.q: Describe respect.
cards.a: Treating others with dignity and valuing them as individuals.

cards.q: Describe Excellence in All We Do and its related virtues.
cards.a: Does not mean that we demand perfection. Directs us to continually advance our craft and increase our knowledge as Air Force professionals. Passion for continuous improvement and innovation to propel accomplishment and performance. On a personal level, Air Force professionals seek out and complete developmental education; work to stay in their best physical, mental, and moral shape. Its related virtues are mission, discipline, and teamwork.

cards.q: Describe mission.
cards.a: A complex undertaking requiring a focus encompassed with operations, product, and resource excellence

cards.q: Describe discipline.
cards.a: Commitment to uphold the highest of personal and professional standards.

cards.q: Describe teamwork.
cards.a: Recognizing the interdependency of every member’s contributions towards the mission and strive for organizational excellence.

cards.q: What are the USSF core values?
cards.a: Character, connection, commitments, and courage.

cards.q: Describe Character.
cards.a:
Defend the Constitution and serve the nation
High moral character and ethical standards
Integrity, grit, honesty, authenticity, trustworthiness
Accountable for decisions, actions, & inactions
Honor obligation to mission, fellow Guardians, loved ones

cards.q: Describe the commitments of character.
cards.a: Act with integrity, honesty, candor, transparency, and dedication to the team. Be accountable to the team for decisions and actions. Uphold the highest standards and live the USSF values.

cards.q: Describe connection.
cards.a: Common purpose greater than ourselves. Stronger together than individually. Embrace a variety of perspectives. Treat everyone with dignity, empathy, respect. Leverage the best each has to offer

cards.q: Describe the commitments of connection.
cards.a: Engage everyone with respect, honesty, and authenticity. Foster an environment that encourages expression and is free from fear. Encourage teammates to share thoughts and talents. Give help when asked and seek assistance when needed.

cards.q: Describe commitment.
cards.a: Pursuit of mastery of self, profession, domain. See opportunities to learn and grow. Make best use of the unique strengths of teammates.

cards.q: Describe the commitments of commitments.
cards.a:
Work to achieve audacious goals. Learn from experience
Seek and offer candid feedback. Facilitate growth and improvement
Embrace challenges. Work to be better tomorrow than today.

cards.q: Describe courage.
cards.a:
Do what needs to be done. Say what needs to be said
Hold to our convictions. Recognize power to choose, regardless of circumstance. Bias toward action. Accept necessary risk to secure & defend domain.

cards.q: Describe the commitments of courage.
cards.a:
Be steadfast and stand up for what is right. Seek opportunities to innovate. Share thoughts and ideas to help the team and mission
Take smart risks.

cards.q: Discuss the importance of the USAF and USSF Core Values to Airmen and Guardians.
cards.a:
Bedrock of leadership in the Air and Space Forces. Institutional values and principles of conduct. Moral framework for military activities
Fundamental and enduring. For Airmen and Guardians, the Core Values help establish the character and professional standards expected of members of the Profession of Arms. Being an Airman or Guardian involves more than simply holding a military position. The lesson describes it as a combination of: 

Profession of Arms + Oaths we swear + Core Values/4 Cs we live by.   For the Space Force specifically, the Guardian Spirit describes the positive attributes expected of members and identifies Guardians as principled public servants, space-minded warfighters, and bold and collaborative problem solvers.

cards.q: Recall the branch of government that establishes military authority.
cards.a: Military authority is derived from the executive branch.

cards.q: List the three US Constitution governing principles.
cards.a:
Federalism
Enumerated Powers
Separation of Powers/Checks and Balances

cards.q: Recall the Amendments to the US Constitution that govern military officer authority
cards.a:
The Bill of Rights — the first ten amendments — places constitutional limits on military authority. 
The Second Amendment prohibits military officers from taking weapons from the public.
The Third Amendment prohibits the military from forcing the public to house them.
The Fourth Amendment prohibits the military from searching the public or other military members without a warrant or probable cause. Military Commanders do control military installations and are allowed to search most areas under their control.
The Sixth, Seventh, and Eighth Amendment prohibits the military officer from punishing members for crimes without a trial.
Article 15s are the exception, but even still, the accused has the right to refuse the Article 15 and demand a Court Martial.
The Nineth Amendment states that just because a right was not mentioned in these Amendments, it doesn’t mean that the government can use this as an excuse to deny these other rights.

cards.q: Summarize the definition of critical thinking.
cards.a: The process of thinking carefully about a subject or idea, without allowing feelings or opinions to affect you.

cards.q: Discuss methods for evaluating information.
cards.a: The first step to evaluating information we receive is to decide whether it is a statement (also called a claim, assertion, or conclusion) or an argument for a given conclusion. Sometimes it can be hard to distinguish between statements and arguments. Statements versus arguments, fact versus opinion, objective versus subjective.

cards.q: Identify the nine intellectual standards used in assessing one’s thinking.
cards.a: Clarity, accuracy, precision, relevance, depth, breadth, logic, significance, and fairness.

cards.q: Explain clarity.
cards.a:
A gateway standard and relevant to all others
“Could you elaborate further?”

cards.q: Explain accuracy.
cards.a:
Addresses the validity of the information at hand
“How can we find out if that’s true?”

cards.q: Explain precision
cards.a:
Helps refine information
“Could you give more details?”

cards.q: Explain relevance.
cards.a:
Evaluates what’s most related to the issue
“How does this relate to our issue?”

cards.q: Explain depth.
cards.a:
Addresses the complexities of an issue
“What are the root causes of this issue, and does this address them?”

cards.q: Explain breadth
cards.a:
Addresses various interpretations of an issue
“Do we need to consider another point of view here

cards.q: Explain logic
cards.a:
Thoughts are mutually supporting and makes sense
“Does this really make sense?”

cards.q: Explain significance.
cards.a:
The most important pieces of an argument or issue
“Which idea or concept is most important?”

cards.q: Explain fairness.
cards.a:
A “gut check” to avoid personal interests, ego, and unjustified assumptions
“What justifies my thinking?”

cards.q: Explain cognitive domain operations and their relationship to disinformation.
cards.a: Take people’s will, belief, thinking, and psychology as direct combat targets, and seek to affect decision-making and actions by changing the opponent’s cognition. It seeks to blend information, psychological warfare, cyberwarfare, and employ its propaganda across the information domain (i.e. social media).

cards.q: Identify the elements of reasoning that are used in the critical thinking process.
cards.a: Purpose, questions, information, concept, inference, assumption, point of view, and implications.

cards.q: Describe the elements of reasoning that are used in the critical thinking process.
cards.a:
Purpose - What is the objective of my thinking?
Question - Is this the right question?
Information - Is it accurate, fair, clear? Are there alternate sources? Do we need more?
Concepts - What concepts (theories, axioms, principles) am I relying on? Do others accept them as well?
Inferences - What am I inferring here that is unstated? Is it valid?
Assumptions - What beliefs and values influence my thinking? Are they balanced and fair?
Point of View - What is my viewpoint? Would it look different from another perspective?
Implications - What might be the outcome? On what? For whom?

cards.q: Discuss common thinking errors that can lead to faulty thinking
cards.a:
System 1 - Fast, instinctive, emotional, unconscious; utilizes pattern recognition
System 2 - Slow, deliberate, logical, conscious; discerns new patterns
Asking the wrong questions (or not asking in the right way) 
Thinking too quickly
Stereotypes
Cognitive bias (halo effect and belief perseverance)
Answering the wrong question - deflection

cards.q: Define problem solving.
cards.a: Purposeful act of observing a problem and then deciding to solve it, after considering solutions and deciding upon one.

cards.q: Compare the 8-step practical problem-solving method to the OODA loop model.
cards.a:
Both models are systematic approaches to solving problems, but they are designed for somewhat different situations. 
8 Steps Process - 1. Clarify and validate the problem. 2. Break down the problem and identify performance gaps. 3. Set improvement targets. 4. Determine root cause. 5. Develop countermeasures. 6. see countermeasures through. 7 confirm results and processes 8. standardize successful processes. 
OODA Loop - 1. Observe. 2. Orient. 3. Decide. 4. Act.

cards.q: Understand the steps for the 8-step practical problem solving method.
cards.a:
1. Clarify and Validate the Problem – Clearly define the problem using objective, specific, and measurable terms. 
2. Break Down the Problem and Identify Performance Gaps – Gather and analyze data to understand the problem and determine the difference between current and desired performance. 
3. Set Improvement Targets – Establish strategic and tactical targets for the desired future state. 
4. Determine Root Cause – Identify the underlying cause rather than simply treating symptoms. 
5. Develop Countermeasures – Analyze possible solutions and select appropriate countermeasures based on effectiveness, feasibility, and impact. 
6. See Countermeasures Through – Implement the solution, monitor progress, use contingency plans, and provide necessary training. 
7. Confirm Results and Process – Use KPIs and metrics to determine whether the solution achieved the intended results. 
8. Standardize Successful Processes – Document successful solutions so the problem is less likely to return and share successful practices.

cards.q: Map the two problem solving models together.
cards.a: Steps 1–2 = Observe; Steps 3–4 = Orient; Step 5 = Decide; and Steps 6–8 = Act.

cards.q: Remember the four stages of growth.
cards.a: 1. Forming. 2. Storming. 3. Norming. 4. Performing.

cards.q: Describe leader and follower actions that contribute to effective teams.
cards.a:
(Forming) "Director" - the team leader should be directive, helping team focus on getting to know one another, identifying members' roles, and clearly understanding the team's mission/tasks
(Storming) "Coach" - team leader who can control the chaos by creating a climate of open discussion, listening to members' concerns, obtaining members' input on how to achieve goals, being encouraging and supportive, and facilitating conflict resolution 
(Norming) "Collaborator" - team leader as a facilitator, focusing on maximizing members' contributions by delegating responsibilities, building members' confidence, and maximizing members' strengths. 
(Performing) "Visionary" - team leader efforts should be on maintaining success and shifting team's perspectives from inward to outward focus by planning for the future, cultivating leadership talent with team, and fostering new ideas from team members, and ensuring solid mechanisms for feedback.

cards.q: Differentiate the characteristics of laissez-faire, transactional, and transformational leadership:
cards.a:
Laissez-faire - Laissez-faire is hands-off leadership and is essentially the absence of leadership. It is an avoidant, non-leadership approach rather than an effective leadership style. 
Transactional - Transactional leadership maintains organizational stability through exchanges between leaders and followers to achieve goals. The leader establishes expectations and uses rewards and/or corrective actions to influence performance. Two examples: Contingent Reward (CR) and Management by Exception (MBE). 

Transformational leadership - Transformational leadership creates personal relationships with followers that raise their level of motivation and morality. Transformational leadership consists of four behaviors/components: Idealized Influence (II), Inspirational Motivation (IM) Intellectual Stimulation (IS), and Individualized Consideration (IC)

cards.q: Describe how to apply FRL.
cards.a:
NOT a continuum from “bad” to “good”
Different circumstances require different approaches
May utilize several approaches at the same time  
Blending and emphasizing approaches is critical

cards.q: Summarize the five basic styles of followership.
cards.a:
Sheep - passive participants and uncritical thinkers; simply comply with any order given; lack initiative; purely reactive; do what they are told, and nothing more. 
Yes people - active participants and uncritical thinkers; dependent on leadership direction; 
Survivors - display qualities of each other type of follower; rarely committed to workplace or group goals; do enough just to get by; seek to minimize interpersonal and intellectual risks
Alienated followers - passive participants and critical thinkers; independent,  capable  of high performance; focus and actions based upon negative experiences; criticize, but rarely offer constructive input
Effective followers - active participants and critical thinkers; independent, intent on high performance; proactive and think ahead; work well with others; reflect on goals of the organization; not hesitant to bring concerns to leaders

cards.q: Distinguish between the characteristics of an effective follower
cards.a:
Support, don’t undermine
Disagree privately
Display initiative
Accept responsibility
Tell the truth
Anticipate boss’s questions
Know their limitations and strengths
Keep boss informed
Selfless in service
Don’t forget their families

cards.q: Distinguish between distributive and integrative approaches to negotiations.
cards.a:
Distributive Negotiation: assumes responsibilities are limited, zero sum-gain perspective leads to competition rather than cooperation; defaults to taking a position (what you want)
Integrative Negotiations: Does not see resources as fixed or zero sum-gain; seeks to achieve solutions and protect relationships; ask about interests (why you want what you want), concerns, limitations.

cards.q: Describe sources of conflict.
cards.a:
Organizational (communications, and structural: rewards and resource independence) 
Personal behaviors (values, perception, and personality)

cards.q: Infer which problem solving-approach to use to best manage conflict in a given scenario.
Identify the problem solving approach evade.
cards.a: "Not now, can you come back later?"

cards.q: Identify the problem solving approach comply.
cards.a: "Yes, absolutely, let's do it your way!"

cards.q: Identify the problem solving approach insist.
cards.a: "Take it or leave it" or "Today - Do it my way!"

cards.q: Identify the problem solving approach settle.
cards.a: "Let's split the difference and call it a day."

cards.q: Identify the problem-solving approach cooperative (Interest-based negotiation)
cards.a: "Let's work together and come up with an even better solution."

cards.q: **Recognize the difference between mission and vision statements. (Know what good and bad ones look like)
cards.a:
Mission (purpose/goal; must have ACTIONs so we know how to accomplish the "what" and the "who") 
Vision (describes the future state of an organization); aspiration/feeling; answers the "why" and "how" - stand alone and straightforward

cards.q: **Recognize a good vision statement (key elements)
cards.a:
Idealistic yet achievable
Articulated well and easily understood
Provides clarity of purpose and direction
Shared and supported

cards.q: Recall the purpose of using the Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, Threats (SWOT) method to identify priorities.
cards.a:
Assess how to use strengths to advantage
Assess how to minimize/overcome weaknesses 
How positive work forces together and potential problems that need to be recognized and addressed

cards.q: Describe techniques for encouraging continued action toward a vision.
cards.a:
Get their attention
Articulate the vision
Frame meaning
Enable action
Reinforce action

cards.q: Recognize Lewin's Change Management model (1940)
cards.a:
Unfreezing 
Changing
Refreezing
*each stage has opportunities and difficulties (driving and restraining forces)

cards.q: Identify common resistance to change.
cards.a:
Distrust
****Uncertainty
Self-Interest
Different Perception/No Felt Need to Change
Over-Determination

cards.q: List the method leaders use to reduce and manage resistance to change.
cards.a:
Remove Obstacles (empowerment); Use the coalition to assist with necessary policy changes to support the change; Instill Knowledge; Develop Ability
Create Short-Term Wins; “Quick-wins” to reach milestones & reduce criticism; Recognize strong performers

cards.q: What are the stages of Lewin's model?
cards.a: Unfreeze, Change, and Refreeze

cards.q: What are some common forms of resistance?
cards.a: Distrust, uncertainty, negative self-interest, different perceptions, and over-determination

cards.q: List some of the responsibilities of a leader in a change effort.
cards.a: Follow the plan, communicate, provide support, remove barriers to change, set short-term and long-term goals, analyze and evaluate changes.
